                                         PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                               §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                            §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                        §                  OF TEXAS
                                                       §


  CRUSOE ENERGY SYSTEMS LLC’S COMMENTS ON STAFF’S SECOND DRAFT
                  DISCUSSION RULE 16 TAC § 25.194

         Crusoe Energy Systems LLC (“Crusoe”) files these comments on the Public Utility
Commission of Texas (“Commission”) second discussion draft rule for 16 Texas Administrative
Code (“TAC”) § 25.194, relating to rulemaking to implement large load interconnection standards
under PURA 37.0561.
                                           I.       INTRODUCTION
         Crusoe is a vertically integrated artificial intelligence (“AI”) infrastructure company that
takes an “energy-first” approach to building solutions. Crusoe appreciates Staff’s time during the
January 9th workshop on Project 58481 (“workshop”) and Staff’s work on the second discussion
draft rule for 16 TAC § 25.194. Crusoe respectfully submits the following comments for
consideration.
                              II.      RESPONSES TO STAFF QUESTIONS
    3. Should the commission maintain the definition for an interconnecting utility that is
       set forth in Attachment C? If not, what definition should be used?
         Crusoe respectfully recommends that the Commission revise the definition of
“interconnecting utility” to distinguish between the roles of the interconnecting transmission
service provider (“TSP”) and the retail distribution service provider (“DSP”) in the large load
interconnection process, as provided in Crusoe’s December 19th comments on the discussion draft
rule (“Crusoe’s Comments”). 1 As explained in Crusoe’s Comments, the interconnecting TSP and
the retail DSP have distinct roles in the large load interconnection process and are often different
entities. To provide essential clarity for this process, the rule should be precise and should
distinguish between the role of the TSP—which is the utility to which the large load customer’s
facilities will connect and the utility that conducts the large load interconnection study (“LLIS”)—

         1
          Crusoe Energy Systems LLC’s Comments on Staff’s Draft Discussion Rule 16 TAC § 25.194 at 5 (Dec. 19,
2025). (Crusoe’s Comments).


HB: 4919-1513-6904.4
 and the role of the retail DSP, which is the utility with the obligation to provide retail electric
delivery service to the large load customer’s load.
        The current proposed definition in Staff’s second discussion draft focuses only on service
area certification by defining “interconnecting utility” as the “electric utility, municipally owned
utility, or electric cooperative that is certificated to serve the interconnecting large load customer
at retail or, if the certificated utility designates, the interconnecting transmission service provider.”
This definition does not provide the necessary clarity as to the distinct roles of the interconnecting
TSP and the retail delivery DSP, which could cause confusion and delays in the LLI process. A
large load customer typically interconnects at transmission voltage to TSP facilities, and the
interconnecting TSP is responsible for the LLIS and constructing any facilities necessary to serve
the requesting large load customer. Rather than limiting the “interconnecting utility” to only the
DSP function, Crusoe proposes that it would be more accurate and reflective of how the LLIS
process works to instead define both roles as part of the “interconnecting utility” role.
        An interconnecting large load customer should provide the required interconnection
request disclosures, enter into the necessary agreements, and pay the study fees, financial security,
and any contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”) directly to the utility that owns and operates
the facilities necessary to interconnect the large load customer to the Electric Reliability Council
of Texas (“ERCOT”) transmission network—that is, the interconnecting TSP. If the retail DSP is
a separate entity, the LLIS process should provide for the large load interconnection request
disclosures to be submitted to the TSP with a copy to the DSP, three-party agreements, and an
option for the large load interconnection customer to pay study fees, financial security, and CIAC
directly to the TSP.

        Accordingly, Crusoe recommends the following modifications to the definitions:

    (6) Interconnecting utility — The distribution service provider and/or the transmission service
    provider. The electric utility, municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that is
    certificated to serve the interconnecting large load customer at retail or, if the certificated utility
    designates, the interconnecting transmission service provider.
    (14) Distribution service provider — the electric utility, municipally owned utility, or electric
    cooperative that is certificated to provide retail electric delivery service to the large load
    customer’s consuming facilities.

    (15) Transmission service provider — the interconnecting utility delegated authority by the
    distribution service provider to act on its behalf for purposes of providing information to
    ERCOT under this section.

                                              Page 2 of 10
                                            HB: 4919-1513-6904.4
        4. If the commission maintains the definition for an interconnecting utility that is set
          forth in Attachment C, what framework should the rule establish for ensuring that
          the interconnecting transmission service provider receives the required security and
          CIAC in instances where the certificated retail utility and interconnecting
          transmission service provider are different entities?
              As discussed in the response to Question 3, Crusoe recommends that the security and CIAC
should be paid directly to the TSP. Where the TSP and DSP are different entities, the large load
customer, the TSP, and the DSP should enter into standardized three-party agreements, allowing
the large load customer to pay the security and the CIAC to the TSP directly. 2

              Crusoe encourages the Commission to explicitly recognize and permit three-party
agreements between a large load customer, an interconnecting TSP, and a retail DSP in the
common situation where the interconnecting TSP is a different entity from the retail DSP.
Providing for three-party agreements will ensure that all relevant parties can efficiently coordinate
their respective obligations and streamline the interconnection process. This avoids making the
DSP the “bank” for a customer’s financial security and CIAC payments for the TSP, and ensures
that the TSP has the necessary funds to proceed with interconnection studies and construction.

       5. For a large load customer that seeks to expand capacity at an existing site, should
          the total capacity or only the new incremental capacity at that site be subject to the
          rule requirements? Why?
              The Large Load Interconnection (“LLI”) process should apply to expansion of load at a
site in two scenarios: (1) if load capacity increases such that it reaches or exceeds the 75 MW
threshold or (2) if a load larger than 75 MW adds capacity in increments of 75 MW or greater.
This approach balances the interests of large load customers with the concerns that ERCOT
expressed in the workshop concerning a potential loophole where a large load customer can submit
a request just under the 75 MW threshold, and then later submit incremental additions that bring
the load over that threshold without going through the LLI process. As ERCOT noted, the rule
should include a time component, so that a large load customer would be required to comply with
LLI requirements if the customer submits load requests for a single site over a certain period that
reaches the 75 MW threshold.

       6. Currently, ERCOT Planning Guide § 9.2.1(1)(b) requires a large load customer to
              follow the criteria subject to the large load interconnection study process if the large

2
    See id.

                                                Page 3 of 10
                                              HB: 4919-1513-6904.4
         load customer modifies an existing load facility that increases the aggregate peak
        demand of the facility by 75 MW or more. Should the commission maintain this
        threshold for purposes of the rule? Or should any modification that increases the
        aggregate peak demand of the facility to 75 MW or more be required to satisfy the
        criteria in the rule?

        To address an increase in demand at an existing load facility, the Commission should
modify the requirement as described in Crusoe’s response to Question 5 above. However, in
general, the Commission should maintain the 75 MW threshold, as Crusoe explained in its
comments on the rulemaking in Project 58480. 3 The 75 MW threshold is widely recognized by
ERCOT stakeholders as the appropriate point at which additional financial security and other large
load regulatory requirements should apply, since this threshold effectively identifies loads with a
material impact on the transmission system. Lowering the threshold would substantially expand
the rule’s applicability to a much broader array of smaller loads, many of which are served at
distribution voltage and do not have a significant effect on the bulk transmission grid.
    7. Does an interconnecting utility, at the intermediate agreement phase, have sufficient
       information to be able to estimate the costs of significant equipment and services and
       to estimate contribution in aid of construction?

            a. If so, should the rule require payment of the $100,000 per megawatt security
               at the time the request for interconnection is submitted? And require
               estimated security for significant equipment and services and contribution in
               aid of construction at the intermediate agreement stage, subject to a true up
               based on actual costs identified at the interconnection agreement stage?
        Crusoe does not believe that the utility has sufficient information at the intermediate
agreement phase to accurately estimate the CIAC. As discussed by representatives from Texas
Industrial Energy Consumers (“TIEC”) and Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”)
during the January 9th workshop, the purposes and timing of financial security and CIAC are
distinct and should be treated accordingly within the rule framework.

        The financial security is intended to demonstrate that a load request is bona fide and to
discourage speculative projects from occupying space in the interconnection study queue. This


        3
          See Project No. 58480, Crusoe Energy System LLC’s Public Reply Comments Regarding Staff’s Proposal
for Publication of New 16 TAC § 37.0561 at 2 (Oct. 31, 2025) (Crusoe’s Reply Comments).

                                               Page 4 of 10
                                             HB: 4919-1513-6904.4
 security should be required only after the initial screening study, at the point where the customer
is prepared to move forward into the LLIS process. As TIEC explained, this early-stage security
functions as a proxy to show that a project is real and committed, even before the utility has
sufficient information to finalize an interconnection agreement or estimate upgrade costs.

       In contrast, the CIAC is meant to cover the estimated costs of upgrades necessary to serve
the requesting load and should only be required after the utility has completed the necessary studies
and can provide a reasonably accurate cost estimate. As both Oncor and TIEC emphasized, at the
intermediate agreement phase, utilities do not yet have the information needed to determine the
full scope or cost of the upgrades that may be required to serve a large load. This is because the
details of required facilities and broader system impacts are not known until the LLIS is completed
and, in some cases, even after a certificate of convenience and necessity process is complete.

       Additionally, Crusoe continues to support a $50,000/MW security as stated in our
December 19, 2025 comments, rather than the newly proposed $100,000/MW in the second
discussion draft. 4 Crusoe believes that a $50,000/MW security is sufficient to aid in eliminating
speculative projects in the load interconnection queue and will improve certainty in calculating
potential load demand for transmission planning purposes. As multiple parties indicated in the
workshop, however, the newly proposed $100,000/MW is excessive and not justified. In some
circumstances, the required security may even greatly exceed actual large load interconnection
costs. This could kill financially viable projects that otherwise meet SB 6’s requirements for
substantiated load. Accordingly, Crusoe urges the Commission to adopt the $50,000/MW security,
which is a reasonable and proportionate security requirement that balances the need to deter
speculative requests with the goal of supporting viable large load projects.

   8. Should the commission expand the criteria for demonstrating site control to include
      either site control over an electrical substation combined with exclusive development
      rights at a designated interconnection point or an exclusivity agreement with an
      existing generation resource for a proposed net metering arrangement?
       Crusoe supports expanding the criteria for demonstrating site control to include either site
control over an electrical substation combined with exclusive development rights at a designated
interconnection point or an exclusivity agreement with an existing generation resource for a


       4
           Crusoe’s Comments at 11.

                                           Page 5 of 10
                                          HB: 4919-1513-6904.4
 proposed net metering arrangement. When a data center is co-located with a generation resource,
it is common for the data center to have an exclusivity agreement with the generator that holds the
option to own or lease land. Recognizing this practice allows these legitimate arrangements to
proceed in the large load interconnection process while still maintaining effective site control
standards that deter speculative load requests.

   9. What value may be gained from collecting data about project developers and end-
      use customers for purposes of developing ERCOT's load forecasts?
       There is little to no value in collecting information about the identity of large load project
developers and end-use customers. This is sensitive commercial information, and aggregate
information about interconnecting large loads is already available. As ERCOT said in the
workshop, ERCOT needs information about installed equipment for modeling and engineering
studies, and information about a large load’s end use for load forecasting purposes. However,
ERCOT does not need to know the end-use customer’s identity and has no purpose for which it
would use that information.

   13. If the commission adopts a process whereby ERCOT, not the interconnecting utility,
       reallocates capacity on a system-wide basis through a batch study process, what
       parameters should the commission establish for such a process?
       Crusoe recommends that if ERCOT adopts a batch study process for system-wide capacity
allocation, it should be conducted twice annually. The process should also prioritize projects that
have demonstrated meaningful progress in the interconnection process. Specifically, the batch
process should utilize a “first-ready, first-served” methodology, rather than a “first-come, first-
served” approach. Under this framework, priority would be given to customers who have satisfied
key interconnection requirements over those who may have submitted an interconnection request
earlier but have not demonstrated substantive project readiness. This approach ensures that
capacity is allocated to projects that are most likely to proceed to construction and operation,
thereby discouraging speculative load requests and reducing the risk of unused or stranded
capacity.

       Additionally, Crusoe recommends that for late-stage large loads, applicants should have
the option to continue working with utilities to meet ERCOT Planning Guide Section 9.5
requirements within the allotted 180 days, or to participate in the initial batch process if ERCOT



                                           Page 6 of 10
                                          HB: 4919-1513-6904.4
 requires additional firming. 5 In such cases, ERCOT should consider alternative evidence of
readiness, such as financial commitments or letters from TSPs. If adopted, ERCOT should not rush
its implementation and should ensure robust stakeholder and commission input, with the initial
Batch Zero large load study beginning no earlier than Q3 of 2026.

    16. Is there anything else that the commission should consider in its implementation of
        PURA §37.0561?
        As stated in Crusoe’s Comments, we recommend adding a definition of “co-located load”
in this rule and/or in the proposed net metering rule in Project 58479. 6 This definition should reflect
that a co-located load is an electrical configuration through which end-use customer load is
physically connected to the facilities of an existing or planned generation resource on the
interconnection customer’s side of the point of interconnection to the transmission system.

        This is consistent with the definition of “co-located load” adopted in other jurisdictions. In
2025, FERC issued orders accepting PJM’s definition of “co-located load” as a configuration
through which end-use customer load is physically connected to the facilities of an existing or
planned generation unit on the interconnection customer’s side of the point of interconnection to
the PJM transmission system. 7 In addition, the FERC Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
defines co-located large loads (called “hybrid facilities”) as loads that share a point of
interconnection with generation facilities. We recommend that the Commission similarly adopt a
definition of co-located load as part of the Senate Bill 6 large load implementation process. 8 Per
Crusoe’s response to this question, Crusoe offers the following additional definitions:

(16) Co-located load — a configuration through which end-use customer load is physically
connected to the facilities of an existing or planned generation resource on the interconnection
customer’s side of the point of interconnection to the transmission system.




        5
            See Planning Guide § 9.4(10).
        6
            Crusoe’s Comments at 5.
        7
          PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115, at P 3 & n.4 (February 20, 2025); PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 164 (December 18, 2025).
        8
         Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large Loads, Proposed Advanced Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, Docket No. RM26-4-000, at P 12 (Oct. 27, 2025)

                                                Page 7 of 10
                                              HB: 4919-1513-6904.4
                                          III.     CONCLUSION
       Crusoe appreciates the Commission’s consideration of these important issues and urges
adoption of a final rule that supports innovation, investment, and reliability in Texas.




Dated January 16, 2026

                                          HB: 4919-1513-6904.4

                                          EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
    •    Discussion Question 3: The Commission should revise the definition of “interconnecting utility”
         to reflect that the interconnecting utility is “the distribution service provider and/or the transmission
         service provider.” The Commission should also add definitions of “transmission service provider”
         and “distribution service provider” to the rule to distinguish the roles of those entities in instances
         where they are separate. This recognizes that in some instances, there is (1) a TSP that owns and
         operates the transmission facilities, and that is responsible for the LLIS and construction of the
         interconnection facilities and (2) a separate retail DSP which is certificated to serve the large load
         customer at retail.
    •    Discussion Question 4: Financial security and CIAC should be paid directly to the TSP. Where
         the TSP and DSP are different entities, a standardized three-party agreement should be used,
         allowing the large load customer to pay the TSP directly. This ensures efficient coordination, avoids
         making the DSP a “bank” for customer money, and ensures that the TSP has the necessary funds
         to proceed with studies and construction.
    •    Discussion Question 5: The LLI process should apply to expansion of load at a site if (1) load
         capacity increases such that it reaches or exceeds the 75 MW threshold or (2) if a load larger than
         75 MW adds capacity in increments of 75 MW or greater.
    •    Discussion Question 6: The Commission should maintain the 75 MW threshold for triggering LLI
         process requirements, as it is widely recognized by ERCOT stakeholders as the appropriate point
         at which additional financial security and progress marker requirements should apply.
    •    Discussion Question 7: A utility does not have sufficient information at the intermediate agreement
         phase to accurately estimate the CIAC. Financial security should be required only after the initial
         screening study, to demonstrate that a load request is bona fide and to discourage speculative
         projects. CIAC should only be required after the utility has completed the necessary studies and
         can provide a reasonably accurate cost estimate. Crusoe continues to support a $50,000/MW
         security as a reasonable and proportionate requirement, rather than the newly proposed
         $100,000/MW.
    •    Discussion Question 8: Crusoe supports expanding the criteria for demonstrating site control to
         include either site control over an electrical substation combined with exclusive development rights
         at a designated interconnection point or an exclusivity agreement with an existing generation
         resource for a proposed net metering arrangement. This expansion recognizes legitimate industry
         practices while maintaining standards that deter speculative load requests.
    •    Discussion Question 9: There is little to no value in collecting information about the identity of
         large load project developers and end-use customers. This is sensitive commercial information, and
         aggregate information about interconnecting large loads is already available. ERCOT has indicated
         that it does not have a purpose for collecting information about the identity of end-use customers.
    •    Discussion Question 13: If ERCOT adopts a batch study process for system-wide capacity
         allocation, it should be conducted twice annually and utilize a “first-ready, first-served”
         methodology. This approach prioritizes projects that have demonstrated meaningful progress in the
         interconnection process and discourages speculative load requests, reducing the risk of unused or
         stranded capacity. Crusoe also recommends that ERCOT not rush implementation, ensure thorough
         stakeholder input, and start the initial Batch Zero large load study no earlier than Q3 2026. Late-
         stage large loads should have the option to continue working with utilities to meet ERCOT Planning
         Guide Section 9.5 requirements within the allotted 180 days, or should be given alternative firming
         options if ERCOT wishes to include those loads in Batch Zero.
    •    Discussion Question 16: Crusoe recommends adding a definition of “co-located load” in this rule
         or in the net metering rule, which defines “co-located load” as “a configuration through which end-
         use customer load is physically connected to the facilities of an existing or planned generation
         resource on the interconnection customer’s side of the point of interconnection to the transmission
         system.”

speculative proj ects in the load interconnection queue and will improve certainty in calculating
potential load demand for transmission planning purposes. As multiple parties indicated in the
workshop, however, the newly proposed $100,000/MW is excessive and not justified. In some

   9. What value may be gained from collecting data about project developers and end-
      use customers for purposes of developing ERCOT's load forecasts?
       There is little to no value in collecting information about the identity of large load project
developers and end-use customers. This is sensitive commercial information, and aggregate
information about interconnecting large loads is already available. As ERCOT said in the
workshop, ERCOT needs information about installed equipment for modeling and engineering
studies, and information about a large load' s end use for load forecasting purposes. However,
ERCOT does not need to know the end-use customer' s identity and has no purpose for which it
would use that information.

    13. If the commission adopts a process whereby ERCOT, not the interconnecting utility,
       reallocates capacity on a system-wide basis through a batch study process, what
       parameters should the commission establish for such a process?
       Crusoe recommends that if ERCOT adopts a batch study process for system-wide capacity
allocation, it should be conducted twice annually. The process should also prioritize projects that
have demonstrated meaningful progress in the interconnection process. Specifically, the batch
process should utilize a "first-ready, first-served" methodology, rather than a "first-come, first-
served" approach. Under this framework, priority would be given to customers who have satisfied
key interconnection requirements over those who may have submitted an interconnection request
earlier but have not demonstrated substantive project readiness. This approach ensures that
capacity is allocated to proj ects that are most likely to proceed to construction and operation,
thereby discouraging speculative load requests and reducing the risk of unused or stranded
capacity.

       Additionally, Crusoe recommends that for late-stage large loads, applicants should have
the option to continue working with utilities to meet ERCOT Planning Guide Section 9.5
requirements within the allotted 180 days, or to participate in the initial batch process if ERCOT

    16. Is there anything else that the commission should consider in its implementation of
        PURA §37.0561?
        As stated in Crusoe's Comments, we recommend adding a definition of"co-located load"
in this rule and/or in the proposed net metering rule in Project 58479.6 This definition should reflect
that a co-located load is an electrical configuration through which end-use customer load is
physically connected to the facilities of an existing or planned generation resource on the
interconnection customer' s side ofthe point of interconnection to the transmission system.

        This is consistent with the definition of "co-located load" adopted in other jurisdictions. In
2025, FERC issued orders accepting PJM' s definition of "co-located load" as a configuration
through which end-use customer load is physically connected to the facilities of an existing or
planned generation unit on the interconnection customer' s side of the point of interconnection to
the PJM transmission system.7 In addition, the FERC Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
defines co-located large loads (called "hybrid facilities") as loads that share a point of
interconnection with generation facilities. We recommend that the Commission similarly adopt a
definition of co-located load as part of the Senate Bill 6 large load implementation process. 8 Per
Crusoe' s response to this question, Crusoe offers the following additional definitions:

(16) Co-located load - a configuration through which end-use customer load is physically

    •    Discussion Question 3: The Commission should revise the definition of "interconnecting utility"
         to re fleet that the interconnecting utility is "the distribution service provider and/or the transmission
         service provider." The Commission should also add definitions of "transmission service provider"
         and "distribution service provider" to the rule to distinguish the roles ofthose entities in instances
         where they are separate. This recognizes that in some instances, there is (1) a TSP that owns and
         operates the transmission facilities, and that is responsible for the LLIS and construction of the
         interconnection facilities and (2) a separate retail DSP which is certificated to serve the large load
         customer at retail.
    •    Discussion Question 4: Financial security and CMC should be paid directly to the TSP. Where
         the TSP and DSP are different entities, a standardized three-party agreement should be used,
         allowing the large load customerto pay the TSP directly. This ensures efficient coordination, avoids
         making the DSP a "bank" for customer money, and ensures that the TSP has the necessary funds
         to proceed with studies and construction.
    •    Discussion Question 5: The LLI process should apply to expansion of load at a site if (1) load
         capacity increases such that it reaches or exceeds the 75 MW threshold or (2) if a load larger than
         75 MW adds capacity in increments of 75 MW or greater.
    •    Discussion Question 6: The Commission should maintain the 75 MW threshold for triggering LLI
         process requirements, as it is widely recognized by ERCOT stakeholders as the appropriate point
         at which additional financial security and progress marker requirements should apply.
    •    Discussion Question 7: A utility does not have sufficient information atthe intermediate agreement
         phase to accurately estimate the CMC. Financial security should be required only after the initial
         screening study, to demonstrate that a load request is bona fide and to discourage speculative
         projects. CMC should only be required after the utility has completed the necessary studies and
         can provide a reasonably accurate cost estimate. Crusoe continues to support a $50,000/MW
         security as a reasonable and proportionate requirement, rather than the newly proposed

         include either site control over an electrical substation combined with exclusive development rights
         at a designated interconnection point or an exclusivity agreement with an existing generation

         practices while maintaining standards that deter speculative load requests.

         large load project developers and end-use customers. This is sensitive commercial information, and

         that it does not have a purpose for collecting information about the identity of end-use customers.
